title: Israeli advertising firm spreading spyware gathered information on Finland’s critical infrastructure
content:
The Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech has distributed fake adverts capable of infecting devices with spyware without the user having to click on the advert. The campaign was revealed by reports published in October by the Citizen Lab research group at the University of Toronto and the cybersecurity firm Confiant.

According to Citizen Lab, this is the first time that such a technique for distributing spyware via advertisements has been publicly exposed. The technique was used to infect devices at Al Jazeera, an international media organisation based in Qatar, amongst others. 

According to the reports by Citizen Lab and Confiant, Discover-Tech collaborates with several spyware manufacturers, such as Candiru and Intelos. The company therefore appears to have been part of an international cyber-espionage operation rather than merely an advertising firm.

title: Where should Poland invest: Time for the Global South?
content:
For the last three decades, Poland’s economic and political strategy was simple: catch up with the West. We focused on integration with the European Union and NATO, which brought us spectacular success. Today, Poland is no longer a poor country – we currently rank around 20th among the world’s largest economies.

However, this success comes at a price. Our development has become dependent on European markets, which are currently struggling with a slowdown. A clear conclusion emerges from the latest, comprehensive report by the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM): if we want to maintain our pace of development, we must look to where the center of gravity of the global economy is shifting. That direction is the Global South.

For many people, this term sounds enigmatic. In the language of diplomacy, it has replaced older terms, often perceived as patronizing, such as the “Third World” or “developing countries.” However, the Global South is about more than just geography. As the authors of the PISM report note, it is primarily a political and economic identity.

title: Czech disinformation groups grow disillusioned with government, remain loyal to far right
content:
Czechia has just held municipal and Senate elections, which brought gains for opposition parties. The Mayors and Independents (STAN), a centrist political movement, performed particularly well, winning in Prague, while numerous candidates backed by the movement succeeded in the Senate elections. The results pose a challenge for the disinformation scene, which has long portrayed STAN as one of its main enemies.

STAN was one of the most frequent targets of disinformation attacks both before and after the elections. According to Bob Kartous, spokesperson for the Czech Elves (Čeští elfové), a group that monitors disinformation on the Czech internet, parts of the scene are now struggling to explain the movement’s electoral success.

“The scene has been consistently and persistently campaigning against STAN for a long time, and as a result, it clearly cannot understand how the party managed to succeed in the elections. A result that does not fit its image of a ‘discredited’ movement is therefore more likely to be explained away as manipulation or the will of ‘the system’ than as genuine support from voters,” Kartous told Update EU.

title: Trump wants to financially cripple the Hague tribunal that issued arrest warrants for Putin and Netanyahu. The EU threatens retaliation
content:
The United States has imposed retaliatory sanctions not only on individual judges and prosecutors but, most recently, on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague as an institution.

Washington is responding to the actions of the Hague judges, who are investigating suspected war crimes in the Gaza Strip and have issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The Hague court serves as the court of last resort for international justice. It prosecutes individuals, including heads of state and military commanders, for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. More than 120 countries recognise its authority. The United States, Russia, China and Israel, however, are not members and reject its jurisdiction.

Washington’s order came on Friday, 9 October 2026, just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize for a UN report concluding that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

title: Preparing for the worst: a single attack could leave us without electricity or heating
content:
Delfi looks at the cyber threats already facing Lithuania’s energy sector and how it is preparing for possible attacks. On 29 December 2025, coordinated cyberattacks targeted more than 30 wind and solar power plants and two combined heat and power plants in Poland. According to CERT Polska, the country’s computer security incident response team, hackers managed to stop a steam turbine and a water treatment system at one of the plants. However, the heat supply to residents was not interrupted. The attacks on the wind and solar plants disrupted their communications with electricity distribution network operators, but power generation continued.

In July 2026, a cyberattack also affected the UK energy sector. According to British media reports, a small electricity generation facility was shut down for four days following the attack. On 7 September, the country’s Energy Minister, Michael Shanks, confirmed that the incident had affected a very small amount of electricity generation, but posed no threat to the wider UK energy system.

title: Europe faces new energy crisis as diesel shortages and fuel prices rise
content:
Russia’s war against Ukraine and tensions in the Middle East have exposed just how dependent Europe remains on energy imports — and how vulnerable it is to turmoil in global markets.

Addressing the European Parliament during its October plenary session, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that gas prices had surged by 140% since the end of February, while diesel prices had doubled. Over the same period, Europe’s fossil fuel import bill had risen by €100 billion.

“Businesses are under severe pressure, people are struggling to pay their bills, and the situation could get worse as winter approaches,” von der Leyen warned. She stressed the need for immediate action to protect those most in need.

“When we import fossil fuels, we also import the shocks and crises that come with them,” she added.

The European Commission argues that Europe must reduce its dependence on fossil fuels and make greater use of clean electricity generated at home. According to Ursula von der Leyen, more than 70% of Europe’s electricity in 2026 comes from domestic low-carbon sources, including renewables and nuclear power.

title: Ukraine disrupts Russian bot networks? The Yandex attacks and disinformation
content:
Charts showing a dramatic drop in Russian bot activity caused a stir on social media. Some suggested that Ukrainian drone strikes had crippled Russia’s propaganda machine, knocking fake accounts used to spread disinformation offline.

But the data tells a different story. The volume of Russian propaganda posts did not decline. Instead, there was a sharp drop in activity by so-called web crawlers – automated programs that scan websites and collect information about their content. That disruption may have affected the reach of propaganda online. But how? Let’s take a closer look.

In recent days, Ukraine has launched a series of strikes against Russian data centres operated by Yandex. On 8 October, drones hit a facility in Sasovo, in Russia’s Ryazan region. Further strikes followed on 9 and 11 October, bringing the total to three attacks on this type of infrastructure.

Yandex is often called Russia’s answer to Google. Alongside its search engine, the company provides email, cloud computing and a range of other digital services.

title: Study Reveals How the European Parliament Uses Fear in Its Climate Communication
content:
Monika Brusenbauch Meislová, an associate professor in the Department of International Relations and European Studies at Masaryk University, examined the European Parliament’s communication during its 9th parliamentary term, from 2019 to 2024. Her study focused on the Parliament’s press releases and posts on X.

“The European Parliament presents itself as an active, responsible and necessary institution that offers solutions, and fear plays a fairly prominent role in building this image,” Brusenbauch Meislová told Update EU.

In 219 of the 235 press releases analysed, there were references to the Parliament’s self-legitimization as a climate actor. More than half of those releases also used fear. On X, fear appeared in approximately one in every seven posts.

The author identified three main narratives in the study. The first is a narrative of urgency, which presents the situation as a crisis requiring immediate action. The second is a narrative of loss, which draws attention to what has already been irretrievably lost or what could still be lost. The third is a narrative of danger, which emphasises future threats and the negative consequences of climate change.

title: Poland Lost PLN 490 Billion Helping Ukraine?
content:
Statistics Poland (GUS) estimated the loss in Poland’s gross domestic product (GDP) between 2022 and 2025 at PLN 490.1 billion (EUR 112,17 bln). The release of these figures quickly became fodder for disinformation. Claims began circulating on social media alleging that this sum represents the direct cost of military and humanitarian aid provided to Kyiv by the Polish government. 

As independent fact-checking organizations such as Demagog determined, this is manipulation based on a selective reading of macroeconomic indicators, intended to stir public sentiment against continuing aid to Ukraine. In reality, GUS’s calculations do not refer to direct financial transfers from the state budget, but to the costs of the economic shock caused by Russia’s invasion of Poland’s eastern neighbor.

title: EU enlargement: Could new members face 15 years of oversight?
content:
The European Commission has presented MEPs with proposals to prepare the EU for a larger membership. The package sets out five areas for reform, from limiting national veto powers and expanding gradual integration to introducing safeguards designed to “hit hard” against countries that breach EU rules after joining. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos argues that new members will not weaken the bloc but help make it fit for the future.

Presenting the Commission’s enlargement package in Strasbourg on 6 October, Kos described it as an “insurance policy” against democratic backsliding following enlargement. The package proposes a time-limited system of safeguards that would subject new member states to special oversight for up to 15 years after accession.

In cases of serious breaches of EU values, the mechanism could allow a country’s voting rights in the Council of the EU to be suspended. Kos said such protections were necessary to “protect ourselves”, pointing to “lessons from previous enlargements”.

For Kos, enlargement is not simply about bringing more countries into the EU. It is also an opportunity to make the Union stronger, more flexible and better equipped to take decisions.
